Who owns which brand, and which engine powers which car

Dozens of car brands. About 15 groups behind most of them.

Jeep, Peugeot and Maserati are siblings. Your Toyota Supra runs a BMW engine. Each bubble below is a parent company, sized by how many vehicles it sold worldwide in 2024. Click one to trace its brands, engines and vehicles.

Bubble area shows approximate 2024 global sales in millions of vehicles, rounded. Groups report differently: Chinese joint-venture sales can count toward both partners, and Toyota's figure includes Daihatsu and Hino. Dashed bubbles are makers selling fewer than about 50,000 vehicles a year, drawn at a minimum size so they stay visible.

Where rival companies work together

Rivals buy engines and platforms from each other

Every line is a working relationship between two companies: one supplies an engine, a hybrid system, an EV platform or a gearbox to the other, or holds a stake in it. Hover a name to see only its links.

Horsepower history

Same engine, different numbers

Automakers retune one engine for each vehicle it goes into: changing the software, turbo boost, intake and exhaust. Pick an engine to see every vehicle and year range it was rated for, or pick a year to compare everything on sale that year.

US-market SAE net horsepower and lb-ft of torque from the makers' published ratings. Diesels sold only outside the US (and BYD) use international ratings converted from kW and Nm. In engine names, "turbo" means one turbocharger and "twin-turbo" means two; engines without either word are naturally aspirated or supercharged (as named). Years with the same rating are grouped. Open-ended imported spans are capped at the 2026 research horizon; they do not independently confirm current availability. Dashed bars show an earlier engine, included so you can compare. Hybrid ratings are combined system output; EV ratings are combined motor output, with usable battery size and EPA range where published. ✓ means a source URL and coverage note are attached to that record. Legacy checkmarks without a recoverable citation are not promoted to this status. Unlinked rows are imported reference claims awaiting individual review, including future-year claims. They are retained for comparison and should not be treated as confirmed specifications. "Sources differ" means reputable sources disagree.

Status as of November 2026. Compiled from manufacturer specifications, public reporting and company announcements. Ratings are US-market SAE net unless a row says otherwise; rows marked ✓ were checked against a published source. Ownership stakes and sales figures are approximate. Field notes summarize widely documented traits and common faults, not every engine's history. Engines and models cover the major ones plus a growing set of rare variants, not every trim or market.
